Muhurat Patti Grading: The First-Flush Launch

A decision case on launch planning

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 12 January 2027, Anwesha Borthakur sat in the Guwahati office of Muhurat Estate Cloud with a printed calendar and a red pen. The first flush of the Assam tea season would begin arriving at factory gates in the second week of March. The annual planters' conference in Guwahati fell on 26 February. Her sales head wanted the company's new leaf-grading module, Muhurat Patti Grading, announced on that stage, with every customer estate offered it at once. Her engineering head wanted to wait. She had to give the company a launch plan by Friday, 29 January, because stall bookings, printing and field travel all closed that day.

2. Company Background

Muhurat Estate Cloud was founded in 2017 by Borthakur, a former estate manager, and two classmates from Jorhat. It sells software to tea estates: daily plucking records by section and plucker, estate labour attendance and wage sheets, and dispatch of green leaf to the estate factory. In January 2027 it served 140 estates at an average of ₹1.8 lakh a year, an annual recurring revenue of ₹252 lakh, or ₹2.52 crore. Of those customers, 62 owned a factory. The company employed 38 people, most in Guwahati, with field engineers in Jorhat and Tezpur.

The market around it was fragmented. Large groups ran ERP systems and Tally Prime for accounts, and packers such as Tata Consumer Products bought graded teas through the Guwahati Tea Auction Centre and private sales. Most small and mid-sized estates still used registers and spreadsheets. The Tea Board of India regulated the sector, and the Plantations Labour Act shaped what labour records an estate had to keep. Muhurat's edge was that its plucking data was already in the customer's hands; leaf grading was the next step along the same chain.

3. The Situation

Muhurat Patti Grading lets a factory clerk photograph incoming green leaf lots and receive a suggested grade, scored on the proportion of two leaves and a bud, coarse leaf and moisture. The head taster remains the authority; the software suggests, and the clerk accepts or overrides. From October to December 2026, four factories ran it in beta. Exhibit 1 shows the result.

4. The People

Anwesha Borthakur, founder and chief executive, Guwahati, must decide. She fears missing the season and also fears a public failure.

Hemanta Saikia, head of sales, Jorhat, holds verbal commitments from 22 of the 62 factory-owning customers. He argues that a conference announcement converts goodwill into signed contracts and that competitors will not wait.

Nayan Hazarika, head of engineering, Tezpur, has watched the beta closely. He wants a smaller start until the module works offline and the match rate rises above 85 per cent.

Tanmoy Bhuyan, data scientist, Toronto, ten and a half hours behind Guwahati in winter, retrains the grading model on the labelled lots. He says accuracy improves with variety, not volume: ten factories with different leaf mixes would teach the model more than forty identical ones would.

5. The Options

Option A: the big bang. Announce at the conference on 26 February and offer all estates the module together, with the ₹45 lakh plan of Exhibit 3. The upside is visibility and 40 signed factories. The cost is that only 20 can go live by 30 June, so half the customers pay for a promise, and the poor Factory D experience could repeat at scale.

Option B: the staged launch. Take six factories live in the first flush, including Factory D after the offline fix, then release in gated cohorts of five factories a month to reach 16 by 30 June, spending ₹18 lakh. The upside is learning across channels before committing money. The cost is a slower headline and possible loss of leads to a competitor.

Option C: delay to the autumn. Skip both flushes, fix the product fully, and launch in August for the autumn flush with a spend of ₹8 lakh. The upside is a polished product; the cost is a lost season and a full year of zero revenue from the module.

6. Questions for Discussion

1. What does the beta data in Exhibit 1 tell Borthakur about the readiness of the product, and which factory should she trust least?

2. Using Exhibit 3, which channels in the big-bang plan generate learning, and which merely spend money before any learning arrives?

3. Why do the signed and live columns in Exhibit 4 diverge for Option A, and who bears that gap?

4. Which option would you take to the board on 29 January, and what would make you change it?

7. A Note for the Learner

This topic frames a launch as a sequence of experiments, not a single event. A big bang commits money, reputation and delivery capacity before the first real evidence arrives. Launch planning schedules the paid, owned and earned channels against what the team has learned, and the common launch mistakes are announcing before delivery capacity exists, spending on all channels at once, and reading signed contracts as live customers.

One defensible path is Option B, run in three gates. Gate 1 in March covers six factories, including Factory D once the offline mode works, and proceeds only if the rolling match rate on the first 500 lots is at least 85 per cent. Gate 2 in April and May adds five factories a month, choosing different leaf mixes as Bhuyan advises, and only opens if support tickets stay within the field team's capacity. Gate 3 in June reviews the cost per live factory against the ₹1.2 lakh first-year price.

The reasoning is direct. Option A's extra ₹4.8 lakh of live revenue costs ₹27 lakh, and 20 of its 40 signed factories cannot be served in time. Option C forfeits both flushes. Under Option B the conference still has a role: a modest demonstration table and Saikia's 22 verbal commitments queued in order of readiness, so sales momentum is kept without promising dates the field team cannot meet. Earned coverage follows real results from Factories A and B, and the owned channels carry the cohort schedule to waiting customers. A strong answer names the gate criteria before the launch, not after it.

Launch Planning and Launch Mistakes: Sizing the First Wave

A launch plan is usually taught as a sequencing problem. It is more usefully understood as a sizing problem under two opposing constraints, layered on top of a commitment schedule that most of the organisation has already signed before the product manager sees it. This page assumes you already accept that staged launches beat big bangs in the general case, and asks the harder questions: how large should the first wave be, what exactly should it be allowed to conclude, when does staging actively destroy value, and who is permitted to stop it.

1. Two rooms, two weeks apart

On the afternoon of 2 September 2026, in a low grey building off the Pune–Bengaluru highway at Hinjawadi, Anirudh Sathe found himself arguing about glue. Sathe was VP of Product at Hridaya Cardiac Systems, a fourteen-year-old medical-device company whose ambulatory ECG patch — a plastic-and-hydrogel rectangle the size of two matchboxes, worn on the chest for up to fourteen days — had been prescribed roughly ninety-six thousand times in the previous financial year by about twelve hundred cardiologists in thirty-eight Indian cities. The patch was not the product, exactly. The product was the patch plus the cloud service behind it: a fleet of analysts in Pune and Coimbatore who read the recorded traces and returned a report to the prescribing cardiologist, typically within forty hours.

Patch 2 was meant to change the economics of that service. An on-device model would pre-classify the trace, flagging the eleven per cent of recording time that plausibly contained an arrhythmia and allowing an analyst to read a fourteen-day study in fifty minutes rather than three hours and ten. Hridaya's gross margin on a study would go from thirty-one per cent to a modelled fifty-four. The board had approved the programme in February. The contract manufacturer at Sriperumbudur had a production slot in the third week of October and a minimum economic run of forty thousand units at ₹1,180 each — ₹4.72 crore of finished goods — against components with a sixteen-week lead time, meaning the purchase orders had in practice been irrevocable since the end of June. The hydrogel adhesive carried a nine-month shelf life from the date of lamination.

The glue was the problem. In July, three of two hundred and forty patches in an internal wear trial had detached at day six or seven rather than lasting the full fourteen. All three failures were on volunteers in Chennai during a fortnight when afternoon humidity did not drop below seventy-eight per cent. Hridaya's quality head, Dr Sunanda Kelkar, would not estimate a field failure rate from three events; she would say only that the true rate was "somewhere between half a per cent and four, and that range is not a useful thing to plan around." The commercial director wanted to launch at the national cardiology congress in the second week of January, a three-day event with about six thousand delegates that Hridaya had used as its principal earned-and-paid moment every year since 2016, and where a competing American patch was expected to make its India debut. Sathe's question was not whether to stage the launch. Everyone in the room agreed that staging was correct. His question was how many patches to put on how many chests before the congress, and what, precisely, that number of chests would entitle him to believe.

Nine days later and eleven hundred kilometres north, Farida Qureshi was having a different argument about a defect nobody would ever report. Qureshi was Chief Product Officer at Hastakshar Systems in Gurugram, a contract-execution platform — signature workflow, clause library, obligation tracking — used by four hundred and thirty enterprise customers across India, Singapore and the Gulf, with about eighty-eight thousand paid seats and annual recurring revenue of ₹96 crore. The top forty accounts, most of them banks, insurers and listed manufacturers, produced sixty-one per cent of that revenue.

Hastakshar Review, the company's first genuinely AI-native module, read an inbound third-party contract and returned a risk summary: unlimited-liability clauses, indemnity caps below policy, auto-renewal traps, governing-law mismatches. In a blind evaluation against a panel of external counsel, Review had caught ninety-four per cent of the issues the panel flagged. It had also, in one type of contract — multi-party vendor agreements with annexures — missed an indemnity cap in one document out of roughly sixty-two.

The launch pressure was a date. Hastakshar's largest channel partner held an annual customer conference in Mumbai on 19 and 20 November; the keynote slot had been offered and provisionally accepted, and the partner's marketing team had already listed "AI contract intelligence" in the printed agenda. Rohit Menon, VP Sales, wanted general availability switched on across all four hundred and thirty tenants on 19 November, arguing that the module's competitive window was six months wide at best and that a tiered rollout would mean his reps were selling something half their accounts could not see. Qureshi's objection was that Review's failure mode was not an outage. It was a confident, well-formatted, wrong answer — and a wrong answer that a general counsel discovered eight months later, in a dispute, would not arrive as a support ticket. It would arrive as a letter. She did not know how to build a gate around a defect that generates no signal.

Both decisions are the same decision, and neither is answered by the standard advice to launch owned-first, earned-second, paid-last. Sathe's cheapest and most controllable channel — direct outreach to his own prescribing cardiologists — is not where his risk lives; his risk lives in the four point seven crore of inventory already committed and in a failure rate he cannot bound. Qureshi's channel sequence is nearly irrelevant; her problem is that her gate metric does not exist. What both need is the layer underneath channel sequencing: a theory of how large an exposure must be before it is informative, how large it may be before it is dangerous, and what to do when those two numbers are in the wrong order.

2. The idea, stated precisely, and the four traditions that disagree about it

Define a launch plan as a schedule of exposures, where an exposure is a pairing of a channel, an audience segment and a volume, each exposure attached to (i) a decision rule stated in advance, (ii) a named individual empowered to act on that rule, and (iii) a remediation branch describing what happens if the rule is not met. The channel-sequencing view — owned, then earned, then paid — is a heuristic that falls out of this definition when reversibility happens to correlate with channel type. It usually does. It does not always, and the cases where it does not are exactly the cases where experienced product managers get into trouble.

The definition's centre of gravity is the word volume. Everything else in a launch plan is comparatively easy to specify: the creative exists, the segments are known, the calendar is visible. Volume is the variable that carries both the information and the risk, and it is the variable that organisations are worst at reasoning about, because the two disciplines that have thought hardest about it — clinical statistics and site-reliability engineering — sit at the two ends of a company that rarely meet.

The practice has four intellectual parents, and they are not friends.

The first is diffusion research: Everett Rogers's 1962 synthesis of how innovations spread through a social system, and Geoffrey Moore's 1991 commercial reworking of it. This tradition contributes the idea that a market is not a homogeneous pool but an ordered set of qualitatively different sub-markets, and that addressing them out of order wastes effort. It is where the instinct to start small comes from, but note carefully what it says: start with a different kind of customer, not with a smaller number of the same kind. A random one per cent sample of your user base is not an early-adopter segment, and treating it as one is a category error that this tradition would never make.

The second is release engineering: the canary release, the feature flag, the percentage rollout, the automated rollback, the error budget. Its texts are operational rather than academic — Jez Humble and David Farley's continuous-delivery work, the site-reliability literature that emerged from large web operations in the 2010s — and its contribution is the insistence that exposure is a dial, that the dial should be turnable downward as fast as upward, and that the decision to turn it should be governed by a pre-agreed budget of acceptable harm rather than by a meeting. This tradition is the source of nearly everything sophisticated in modern launch practice, and it has one blind spot: it assumes the harm is observable within the rollout window.

The third is integrated marketing communications and the brand-science school associated with Andrew Ehrenberg and, more recently, Byron Sharp's work at the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute. This tradition holds, on the basis of a large and genuinely robust empirical record about how brands grow, that reach is the dominant variable, that light and non-buyers matter more than enthusiasts, and that mental availability is built by broad, simultaneous, repeated exposure. It regards the staged launch with real suspicion, and not out of stupidity: a launch is the one moment when a product has novelty, and novelty is the raw material that earned media converts into free reach. Spend it in slices and you may find that when you finally want the coordinated moment, there is nothing left to coordinate around.

The fourth is validated learning, the Blank–Ries lineage, which reframes the launch as an experiment rather than an announcement. Its contribution is the insistence that a launch should be designed to produce a decision, and that a launch which could not have produced a "no" was never an experiment at all. Its characteristic failure is to treat all information as equally valuable and all experiments as cheap, which is a reasonable assumption for a pre-revenue software startup and an unreasonable one for a company with ₹4.72 crore of hydrogel ageing in a warehouse.

TraditionWould signWould refuse to signRests on

The competent practitioner picks one tradition and applies it. The expert holds all four and knows which one the situation is in. Sathe's situation is governed by release engineering with a diffusion overlay — he needs a harm budget, and he needs his first wave to be a chosen segment of high-tolerance cardiologists rather than a random draw. Qureshi's situation is governed by validated learning, because her real problem is that she does not yet know the thing she would need to know to write a gate. And both of them have a brand-science constituency inside the building — the commercial director at the congress, Menon at the partner keynote — whose objection is not foolish and will not be defeated by being called a big-bang thinker.

3. Mechanics: the two constraints that set wave size

Begin with the constraint the release-engineering tradition never states explicitly, because in software the sample sizes are large enough that it is never binding: a wave that is too small cannot see the defect it is supposed to catch.

Suppose a defect occurs independently with probability p in each exposed unit. If you expose n units and observe zero occurrences, the probability of that happening by chance when the true rate is p is (1 − p)n. Setting that equal to five per cent and solving gives the familiar rule of three: n ≈ 3 / p. A clean wave of three hundred units tells you, at ninety-five per cent confidence, that the defect rate is below one per cent. It tells you nothing whatever about whether the rate is 0.1 per cent or 0.9 per cent, and a manager who treats "we saw no failures in three hundred" as evidence of a safe product at forty thousand units has confused the absence of evidence with an upper bound that is not tight enough to matter.

That distinction — between detecting a defect's existence and measuring its magnitude — is the single most useful piece of arithmetic in launch planning, and it is where Sathe's argument about glue resolved itself. Measuring a proportion to within a stated precision requires roughly n = 3.84 × p(1 − p) / d2, where d is the half-width of the confidence interval you are willing to live with. The numbers diverge violently.

Kelkar's refusal to name a number now becomes tractable. Hridaya's decision-relevant threshold was two per cent: above that, the field-service burden made Patch 2's margin improvement illusory and, more seriously, tripped the company's internal rule for notifying a device incident trend to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. To distinguish "below two per cent" from "above two per cent" with reasonable confidence required somewhere around eleven hundred to fifteen hundred patches worn to completion, in conditions that included the hot-humid coastal environments where the three failures had occurred. Not three hundred. Not, as the commercial director had proposed, "a couple of hundred with our best accounts in Pune" — a wave that was both underpowered and drawn from precisely the climate in which the defect does not express.

Now the opposing constraint. Let c be the cost per affected unit, including the part that is not money, and let B be the harm budget — the total loss the organisation has decided in advance it can absorb from this wave without the launch becoming a corporate event. The blast-radius ceiling is n ≤ B / (pmax × c), where pmax is the pessimistic end of your prior, not the expected value. Hridaya set B at ₹25 lakh of direct cost, on the reasoning that anything larger would require a board disclosure and would therefore stop being a product decision. With pmax at four per cent and c at ₹3,400, the ceiling was 25,00,000 / (0.04 × 3,400) = 18,382 units.

With the band established, three further mechanics follow, and they are the steps most plans leave implicit.

Escalation ratio and calendar cost. Once the first wave is sized, the rest of the plan is a geometric series. If each wave multiplies exposure by a factor k, the number of waves needed to reach a population N from a first wave n1 is log(N/n1) / log k, and the calendar cost is that number multiplied by the gate latency — the time it takes the deciding signal to become legible. For Hridaya: N of forty thousand, n1 of twelve hundred, gate latency of eighteen days because a fourteen-day wear study plus reporting cannot be hurried. At k = 4, that is log(33.3)/log(4) = 2.53, so three further waves, four in total, seventy-two days. At k = 8, it is 1.69, so two further waves, three in total, fifty-four days — eighteen days saved at the price of an eightfold rather than fourfold jump in exposure at each step. Sathe's real negotiation with the commercial director was never about staging versus big bang. It was about k, and about eighteen days.

Gate latency is a design variable, not a fact. Competent practitioners choose the most important metric and wait for it. Experts choose the metric with the best ratio of information to latency and instrument a leading indicator beside it. Hridaya could not shorten the fourteen-day wear period, but it could — and did — add a daily adhesion telemetry ping from the patch, so that a rising rate of impedance anomalies on day four would predict a detachment on day six. That changed the effective gate latency for the abort decision from eighteen days to five, while leaving the gate latency for the proceed decision at eighteen. Asymmetric gates — fast to stop, slow to go — are the mark of a plan written by someone who has been burned.

The remediation branch. A threshold with no pre-written response to failure is not a gate; it is a number on a slide. When a wave misses its threshold, the organisation is under maximum time pressure and minimum cognitive capacity, and the choice it makes will be whichever option was already written down. Hridaya's plan specified three branches before Wave 1 opened: below one per cent detachment, proceed at k = 8; between one and two per cent, proceed at k = 3 with a revised patient-instruction insert and a pre-approved free-replacement policy; above two per cent, stop, notify the twelve hundred prescribers within seventy-two hours using a communication Kelkar had already cleared, and switch the congress plan from a product launch to a clinical-data session on the existing patch. Writing the third branch in August cost an afternoon. Writing it in January would have cost the company its reputation with the only twelve hundred customers it has.

4. Conditions of application, stated as testable claims

The general case for staging rests on four propositions. Each is testable against a specific situation, and each fails in identifiable circumstances. Applying them to Sathe and Qureshi shows how differently the same doctrine lands.

Table 3. Four claims that must all hold for a staged launch to dominate a coordinated one, tested against both protagonists.
ClaimHridaya (Patch 2)Hastakshar (Review)
C1. The defect, if present, expresses at small scale. The failure mechanism does not require volume, concurrency or time-in-market to appear. Holds, conditionally. Adhesive failure is a per-unit event — but only in hot, humid conditions, so the wave must be chosen for climate, not convenience. Fails as stated. The miss rate is a per-document event, but it expresses only against ground truth, which does not exist unless someone pays for it.
C2. Value does not depend on the density of the wave itself. A user in a five-per-cent wave gets the same product as a user at full scale. Holds cleanly. A patch on a chest works identically whether twelve hundred or forty thousand are in the field. Holds. Review is single-tenant in its value; no network effect.
C3. The upstream commitments are themselves stageable. Money and capacity can be released in tranches matched to the waves. Fails. ₹4.72 crore of inventory and a sixteen-week component lead time were committed in June. The waves stage exposure; they cannot stage the bet. Holds. Compute and evaluation spend scale with enablement; the only hard commitment is the partner keynote slot.
C4. Novelty survives the schedule. The coordinated moment you are deferring will still be available and still be new when you reach it. Contested. The congress happens once a year; a competitor is launching into the same room; novelty is perishable on a fixed annual clock. Fails. A tiered rollout that reaches fifteen per cent of accounts by 19 November means the keynote either misrepresents availability or is given up.
Where C1 or C2 fails, staging produces misinformation. Where C3 fails, staging produces the illusion of control. Where C4 fails, staging has a real and quantifiable cost that must be set against the harm it avoids.

Two of these deserve emphasis because they are the ones practitioners systematically discount.

C3 — the stageability of upstream commitments — is the claim that most often fails silently, and it is why launch planning taught purely as channel sequencing produces managers who feel safe while standing on a large unhedged bet. Hridaya's four-wave plan is a genuinely good plan and it does not reduce the company's financial exposure by a single rupee. The forty thousand units exist; the hydrogel is ageing; if Wave 1 shows a three per cent detachment rate, the inventory is worth its scrap value regardless of how elegantly the waves were sequenced. What staging buys Hridaya is not money. It is the difference between discovering the problem across twelve hundred patients whose cardiologists can be telephoned individually and discovering it across twelve thousand, which is a regulatory event. That is a real and large benefit. It is not the benefit the plan appears to promise, and confusing the two is how a product manager comes to believe a launch is de-risked when only its reputational tail has been trimmed.

C4 — the survival of novelty — is where the brand-science objection is strongest and where the staging orthodoxy is weakest. There is a real asset called the first time anyone hears about this, it is consumed on use, and a staged plan spends it in the cheapest channel first. Journalists, analysts and conference programme committees all apply a recency test; a product that has been quietly live for four months is not a story. Hridaya's commercial director was not being reckless when he wanted the congress; he was observing, correctly, that the difference between launching Patch 2 at the congress and launching it in March was the difference between six thousand cardiologists encountering it in a room designed to make them pay attention and a direct-mail campaign to the same people. An expert does not dismiss this. An expert prices it, and then designs the waves so that something genuinely new remains for the coordinated moment — which in Hridaya's case meant holding back the published fourteen-day adhesion data and the pricing change for the congress, and running the early waves as a clinical pilot programme rather than as a launch.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the organisational seams

The doctrine bends in five recognisable situations, and in each case mature companies handle it in a way that differs from what their own playbooks say.

Two-sided marketplaces. Hathkargha Haat, a Varanasi-based platform matching handloom weaver clusters to apparel buyers and interior brands, learned the standard lesson the standard way: a fraction-of-the-base wave on a marketplace does not produce a small marketplace, it produces a broken one. Demand that arrives to find four hundred SKUs instead of forty thousand does not come back, and the churn it generates is permanent, not recoverable when supply catches up. Hathkargha's eventual method — and it is the method essentially every marketplace converges on — was to stage by cell rather than by fraction: one district's weavers, fully saturated, before any buyer-side channel opened in that category at all. The published playbook said "phased rollout." What the company actually did was run a series of small, complete big bangs, each within a boundary chosen so that liquidity inside the boundary was real. The generalisable rule: when value depends on density, the unit of staging must be a self-sufficient market, not a sample.

Regulated products with externally fixed dates. Hindol Energy Systems, which supplies meter-data management software to three state electricity distribution utilities, has almost no discretion over launch timing. When a state regulator issues a tariff order effective on the first of a month, every consumer in the state must be billed on the new slab structure from that date; there is no version of the launch in which eight per cent of consumers get the new tariff. Hindol's staging therefore happens entirely inside the building: shadow-billing runs in which the new engine computes bills in parallel with the old one for six full cycles without any consumer seeing the output, followed by a single mandated cutover. This is a genuinely different discipline, and it is worth naming because product managers coming from consumer software routinely misdiagnose it as organisational cowardice. It is not. When the exposure cannot be staged, the verification must be, and the skill shifts from wave design to building a parallel environment faithful enough that its results transfer. The failure mode is correspondingly different: not a bad launch but a shadow environment that quietly diverges from production, so that six clean cycles prove nothing.

Hardware plus software. Hridaya's case is the general one: the software is stageable and the hardware is not, and the two halves of the product therefore live on different risk clocks. The seam shows up organisationally as a supply-chain director who committed in June and a product manager who is designing waves in September, neither of whom has ever attended the other's planning meeting. The practice that distinguishes good hardware companies is a single joint document — Hridaya calls it the commitment ladder — that lists every decision by the date after which it cannot be reversed and the amount it costs to reverse it before that date, and which is reviewed at the same cadence as the launch plan. Most companies discover they need this after their first write-off.

AI-native products. Qureshi's problem generalises to a whole class. When the failure mode is a wrong output rather than a failed one, three of the launch planner's usual instruments break simultaneously. Support-ticket volume stops being a signal, because users do not report answers they believe. Usage stops being a signal, because a confidently wrong system is pleasant to use. And the gate itself acquires a price, because establishing whether the output was right requires an expert to look at it. Hastakshar's evaluation of Review cost ₹900 per contract in external counsel time, which meant that the statistically adequate wave — twelve hundred labelled multi-party agreements, enough to distinguish a 3.1 per cent miss rate from a 1.1 per cent one — carried a line item of ₹10.8 lakh before any customer saw anything. The mature response, which Hastakshar adopted, is to treat evaluation capacity as the scarce resource the launch schedule is built around, exactly as a hardware company treats production capacity. The immature response, extremely common in 2026, is to ship to everyone, add a thumbs-down button, and call the resulting trickle of self-selected complaints a quality programme.

Multi-product companies and the calendar cartel. The last edge case is purely organisational. In a company with six product lines, the launch calendar is a scarce shared resource: there are only so many keynote slots, press moments and field-enablement weeks per year, and they are allocated politically, usually a year in advance. A product manager who discovers in month nine that her feature is not ready is not merely delaying her own launch; she is releasing a slot that three other teams want, and she will not get it back. This is the real mechanism behind most launches that go ahead despite known defects, and it is almost never described honestly in retrospectives, which prefer the more flattering explanation of optimism bias. Companies that handle it well do one specific thing: they decouple the slot from the product by booking the slot to a theme rather than a feature, so that a launch can slip without the slot being lost.

6. Ten nuances that separate the expert from the competent

1. The expert asks "what rate of what defect?" before asking "what percentage of users?"
A competent practitioner opens the conversation with a rollout percentage — one per cent, five, twenty-five — which is a number borrowed from software deployment convention and carries no information about the product at hand. The expert's first question runs backward from the failure she is trying to see: what could go wrong, how often would it happen if it were going wrong, and how many units must therefore be exposed before its absence means anything. The tell-tale sign in a meeting is a plan whose wave sizes are round percentages. Real wave sizes are awkward numbers, because they are derived. The obvious reading — that a small percentage is inherently safer — is wrong in a specific way: a wave too small to detect the defect is not safe, it is merely uninformative, and it converts into false confidence the moment someone says the first wave "went fine."
2. Gate metrics are chosen for latency, not importance.
The metric that matters most for Patch 2 is ninety-day prescriber repeat rate. It is useless as a gate because it arrives in April. The expert selects the earliest observable variable that is causally upstream of the thing that matters and is sensitive enough to move, then states the assumed link explicitly so it can be challenged. The tell-tale sign of expertise is a plan that names both numbers: the decision metric and the outcome metric it stands in for. The obvious reading — gate on what matters — is wrong because a gate that resolves after the decision has been forced is not a gate; it is a post-mortem.
3. The real unit of staging is commitment, not audience.
An expert reads the procurement calendar, the hiring plan and the media-booking terms before reading the channel plan, because those documents contain the decisions that cannot be unwound. The tell-tale sign is a product manager who can answer, without looking it up, the date after which each major commitment becomes sunk and the penalty for reversing it the day before. The obvious reading — that a staged launch reduces exposure — is wrong whenever the exposure was created upstream: Hridaya's waves reduce reputational and regulatory risk substantially and financial risk not at all, and a manager who cannot say which is which will over-trust the plan.
4. Novelty is a depleting inventory with a use-by date.
Experts treat attention the way a hardware company treats a scarce component: they know how much they have, they know what each wave consumes, and they refuse to spend the last of it on a channel that cannot convert it. The tell-tale sign is a launch plan with an explicit answer to "what will still be new in November?" — usually a data set, a price change, a named customer or an availability milestone deliberately withheld from the early waves. The obvious reading — that early waves are small and therefore consume little novelty — is wrong, because novelty is destroyed by disclosure, not by volume. One blog post read by four hundred people can make a product ineligible for coverage six months later.
5. A gate without a written "no" branch is decoration.
The expert writes the failure path first, in detail, including who signs the customer communication and what the fallback narrative for the launch moment will be. The tell-tale sign is that the "no" branch has a named owner and a drafted artefact, not a placeholder. The obvious reading — that writing failure plans is pessimism — misunderstands the mechanism: the branch is not written to predict failure but to remove the decision from the moment when the organisation is least capable of making it, which is the hour the bad number arrives.
6. Reversibility is two numbers, and they are not correlated the way people assume.
Every channel has a commitment lead time — how far in advance the money or the promise becomes irrevocable — and a recall half-life — how long the message persists after you try to withdraw it. Experts plot both. The tell-tale sign is someone classifying an unpaid creator video as less reversible than a purchased television slot: the TV buy is expensive and inflexible but its recall half-life is close to zero once the flight ends, whereas the creator video is cheap, flexible and permanent, screenshot and re-uploaded beyond any possibility of correction. The obvious reading — paid is irreversible, owned is reversible — is a serviceable first approximation that fails precisely where modern launches actually live.
7. Staging biases what you learn, and the bias has a known sign.
The first wave is almost never a random sample of the eventual population. It is composed of the most engaged users, the friendliest accounts, the cardiologists who answer the phone — people selected, implicitly or explicitly, for tolerance. Their conversion, retention and satisfaction are therefore upward-biased, and their defect-reporting rate is upward-biased too, which pulls in the opposite direction. The expert names an enthusiasm discount before the wave runs — "we expect Wave 1 activation to be 1.6 to 2 times the steady-state rate, so a 1.4-times result is a warning, not a success" — and holds herself to it. The tell-tale sign is a plan that states the expected wave-over-wave decay. The obvious reading — that a good Wave 1 predicts a good Wave 3 — is wrong in the direction that gets budgets approved, which is why it survives.
8. The binding constraint is usually internal capacity, not market risk.
Ask an expert how she arrived at a wave size and she will frequently give an operational answer before a statistical one: the support team absorbs ninety additional tickets a day, the wave generates 0.11 tickets per exposed user, the gate takes fourteen days, therefore the wave cannot exceed about eleven thousand users without degrading service to everyone else. The tell-tale sign is a launch plan that contains a staffing table. The obvious reading — that capacity planning is an operations concern downstream of the launch decision — inverts the actual dependency: in most companies the queue is the constraint, and a launch that overruns it converts a product problem into a service problem that outlives the launch by a quarter.
9. Some gates cost money to observe, and observability belongs in the launch budget.
For most consumer software the gate is free: the telemetry already exists. For AI products, regulated products, hardware and anything sold through a distributor, establishing the truth costs something real — expert labelling, field inspection, secondary-sales audit, a mystery-shopper programme. Experts put a line item for it in the launch budget and defend it when finance cuts. The tell-tale sign is a budget in which evaluation is a named cost rather than an assumption. The obvious reading — that measurement is overhead — gets the accounting backwards: an unobservable gate converts a staged launch into a big bang with extra meetings, at full cost and with none of the benefit.
10. Silence has a false-negative rate, and experts estimate it.
"No complaints" is a measurement, and like any measurement it has a sensitivity. If eight per cent of users affected by a given problem would report it, then zero reports from a wave of a thousand users is consistent with as many as thirty-seven affected users at ninety-five per cent confidence. The expert computes this and says so. The tell-tale sign is someone asking, of a clean support queue, "what fraction of people hit by this would actually tell us?" — and then, having answered perhaps five per cent, refusing to treat the queue as evidence. The obvious reading — that a quiet launch is a good launch — is the single most expensive misreading in the discipline, and it is getting more expensive as the products being launched become ones whose failures are invisible to the people experiencing them.

7. How the practice actually differs by product type and company stage

The doctrine is often presented with a matrix of differences across consumer, B2B, enterprise, marketplace, hardware and AI. Much of that matrix is decoration. It is worth saying plainly where the difference is real and where it is not.

What does not differ. The arithmetic of detection is identical everywhere. A one-in-sixty defect requires roughly a hundred and eighty exposures to be seen once whether the exposed thing is a chest, a contract or a checkout. The requirement that the gate be written before the wave opens does not differ. The requirement that someone be empowered to say no does not differ. The tendency of finance calendars to push toward big bangs does not differ. Practitioners who believe their domain is special usually mean that their domain is unfamiliar to the person giving them advice.

Consumer. The genuine difference is that the population is large enough that statistical constraints almost never bind — any wave big enough to be operationally interesting is big enough to be statistically adequate — and the binding constraint moves entirely to support capacity, fraud exposure and, for network-dependent features, density. Consumer is also the only category where true randomised holdouts are cheap, which means the consumer practitioner has an instrument the others lack and should use it: a permanent five per cent holdout carried through every wave converts the whole launch into a measurable experiment rather than a before-and-after story.

B2B and enterprise. Here the wave is a named list, not a fraction, and the gate is usually about the seller rather than the buyer. Hastakshar's real Wave 1 gate was not customer usage; it was whether eleven of Menon's fourteen enterprise reps could deliver the Review demonstration to a live prospect without a solutions engineer on the call. That is a capability gate, it takes three weeks to observe, and if it fails the launch cannot proceed no matter how good the product is, because in enterprise the channel is the sales force and an untrained sales force mispositions a product in ways that take two renewal cycles to correct. The second genuine difference is that enterprise customers have their own change-management calendars; a tenant that has frozen changes for quarter-end cannot be in your November wave regardless of your plan.

Platforms and marketplaces. Discussed above: the unit of staging is a self-sufficient market cell. The additional wrinkle at platform scale is that third-party developers are a third side, with lead times of their own; a platform capability launched to developers and users simultaneously will be judged on an ecosystem that has had no time to build for it.

Hardware and physical goods. Two commitments dominate: manufacturing and distribution. Harivansh Foods, an Indore-based millet-snack brand, illustrates the second. Its route to market ran through a distributor network into roughly forty-two hundred outlets across three states, and the minimum viable unit of a distribution launch is one distributor's territory — you cannot ask a distributor to stock eleven per cent of his outlets. Harivansh's primary billing of ₹2.9 crore was therefore committed before a single consumer had bought a packet, and the number that mattered, secondary sell-through, was invisible for eight weeks and then came in at eighteen per cent against a plan of forty-five. In physical goods the launch plan's centre of gravity shifts from channel sequencing to sell-through instrumentation: the discipline is not staging the exposure, which cannot be staged, but buying visibility into what happens after the trade load, through retail audits and outlet-level scanning, fast enough to stop the next production run.

AI products. The distinctive feature, already discussed, is silent failure. The second distinctive feature is that the product changes without a release: a model update, a prompt change, a retrieval index refresh can alter behaviour for every user at once, which means an AI product has a continuous, invisible big bang running underneath whatever launch plan sits on top. Companies that handle this well treat every model change as a launch with its own wave plan and its own gate. Companies that do not will eventually discover that their carefully staged feature launch was undone by a silent upgrade of the underlying model three weeks later.

Stage. The change with company stage is less about technique than about which error is cheap. A seed-stage company's dominant risk is irrelevance, not harm; its optimal launch is closer to a big bang than the doctrine suggests, because it has no reputation to damage, no installed base to disrupt, and a desperate need for the information that only real exposure provides. A growth-stage company has the worst of both: an installed base large enough that harm is expensive, and a market position insecure enough that delay is expensive too — this is where wave design earns its keep, and where most of the interesting judgement lives. A large public company has an asymmetry that is rarely stated honestly: the downside of a bad launch is a headline and possibly a regulatory letter, the upside of a good one is a rounding error on revenue, and therefore its launch machinery is calibrated for harm avoidance to a degree that would be irrational anywhere else. Product managers who move from a startup to a large company and complain about launch bureaucracy are usually failing to notice that the payoff matrix genuinely changed.

Hullor: where staging produced the wrong answer

Hullor, a Kolkata-based regional-language community app with about 4.1 million monthly actives across Bengali, Assamese, Odia and Bhojpuri, launched a live group-audio feature called Rooms in 2025 under a textbook staged plan. Wave 1 went to a randomly sampled three per cent of the base, roughly 123,000 users, with a pre-written gate: at least eighteen per cent of exposed users must join a room within fourteen days, and median session length must exceed nine minutes.

The wave produced 4.6 per cent join rate and a median session of eighty seconds. The gate closed. Rooms was killed in week five and the team reassigned. Eleven months later a competitor launched an almost identical feature to its entire base at once and it became the single largest driver of session growth in that company's year.

The arithmetic of the failure is worth doing, because it is not a story about courage. Hullor's audience partitions into roughly 140 language-and-interest cells — Bengali devotional music, Bhojpuri comedy, Odia job-seekers and so on — and a live audio room is only worth entering if someone is talking in it. Three per cent of 4.1 million is 123,000, which across 140 cells is 879 users per cell. At a twelve per cent feature-adoption rate and thirty minutes of daily use, expected concurrency in a cell is 879 × 0.12 × (30/1440) = 2.2 people. At full exposure the same calculation gives 29,285 × 0.12 × (30/1440) = 73 people. Hullor's own prototype research had established that a room becomes self-sustaining somewhere above fifteen concurrent listeners. The staged wave was therefore operating a full order of magnitude below the threshold at which the product exists at all. It did not measure Rooms. It measured an empty room.

The recovery, when Hullor eventually rebuilt the feature in 2026, changed one thing: the wave was defined by cell rather than by user. Two cells — Bengali devotional music and Bhojpuri comedy — were exposed at one hundred per cent, about fifty-nine thousand users in total, which is fewer users than the failed wave but produced concurrency of sixty-one and seventy-four respectively. Join rate was twenty-three per cent; median session eleven minutes. The lesson Hullor's product leadership drew, and which is the correct one, is that C2 from Table 3 must be tested explicitly before any percentage-based wave is designed, and that the test is a single question: does a user in this wave get the same product as a user at full scale? For anything with a live, social or liquidity component the answer is no, and a percentage rollout will generate a confident, well-instrumented, entirely false negative. Staged launching has a type-two error rate, it is rarely discussed, and it kills good products quietly.

Two of these deserve a further sentence because they are the ones that hide inside good plans. Gate drift is invisible in any single meeting and obvious across four; the only reliable defence is a document with an audit trail and a habit of reading the original number aloud at the start of each gate review. The authority vacuum is the failure that the staged-launch literature almost never addresses, because it is not a planning problem but a governance one. A wave plan distributes the decision to stop across three or four review points, and unless one person owns each of them, what the plan has actually created is four opportunities for a group to fail to act.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disputes in this field are live, and none of them is resolved by a synthesis. Each is stated here in the strongest form its adherents would recognise.

Dispute one: does staging destroy more value through novelty leakage than it saves through harm avoidance? The brand-science position, steelmanned, is this: growth comes overwhelmingly from reach among light and non-buyers; a product's launch is the single cheapest reach it will ever have access to, because novelty converts into earned coverage at a rate no media budget can match; and staged launches systematically spend that novelty on the audience least in need of persuasion — the installed base — while arriving at the coordinated moment with a product that is no longer news. The evidence is the penetration-versus-loyalty literature and a long record of category winners who were not first but were loudest. The staging position replies that harm is not symmetric with foregone reach: a failed launch can cost a regulated company its licence, and a bad first impression among the installed base is not recoverable by any amount of subsequent reach. What would have to be true for the brand-science position to be wrong in a given case: that the defect risk is non-trivial and that the harm from it is non-linear in exposure. What would have to be true for the staging position to be wrong: that defect risk is genuinely low and that the category has a winner-take-most dynamic in which a six-month lead in mental availability is decisive. Both conditions are checkable in advance, which is why this dispute is tractable in the particular even though it is intractable in general.

Dispute two: are pre-committed gates a commitment device or an invitation to gaming? The pro-gate position is straightforward and well evidenced: humans evaluate ambiguous results in the direction of their incentives, and the only defence is a number written before the incentive exists. The anti-gate position, which is held by serious people and is not laziness, runs as follows: once a threshold is written down, the organisation optimises for the threshold rather than the underlying reality — a textbook Goodhart effect — and teams will choose gate metrics for their gameability, will construct waves whose composition flatters the metric, and will treat clearing the gate as permission to stop thinking. On this view the honest alternative is a qualitative stop-rule owned by a named individual with explicit authority and no numeric target: "Kelkar decides whether the adhesion data is good enough, and Kelkar's judgement is the gate." The evidence for this position is the observable behaviour of organisations with elaborate gate frameworks, which frequently ship worse products than organisations with one trusted engineer who can halt a release. For the numeric-gate position to be wrong, it would have to be true that the gaming losses exceed the confirmation-bias losses — which is more plausible in organisations with strong individual accountability and less plausible in large, diffuse ones. Most practitioners who have worked in both kinds of company change their view on this question when they change employers, which should tell us something.

Dispute three: is clean attribution worth its calendar cost? The sequencing tradition insists on isolated windows so that each channel's effect is separable. The measurement tradition — marketing-mix modelling, geographic holdouts, incrementality testing — argues that channel-level attribution from sequential windows is an illusion anyway, because effects are lagged, non-linear and interacting, and that a launch which runs all channels simultaneously across randomised geographies will produce a far better causal estimate in less time than a sequence of confounded single-channel windows. The steelman of the measurement position is strong: a staged launch is a time series with one observation per channel and no control, which is close to the weakest design in the empirical repertoire, while a geo-split launch is a randomised experiment. What would have to be true for the measurement position to be wrong: that the product has enough defect risk that running everything at once is unacceptable regardless of measurement quality, or that the business is too small or too geographically concentrated for geo-splits to have power. Both are often true in India, where a single metropolitan market can be a third of demand, which is why the dispute lands differently here than in the United States.

Dispute four: should launches exist at all in a continuous-delivery organisation? One camp holds that "launch" is a vestige of the boxed-software era, that features should reach users continuously behind flags, and that the coordinated announcement is a marketing artefact that should be fully decoupled from engineering reality — ship whenever, announce whenever, and never let the two constrain each other. The other camp holds that customers, sales forces, partners and journalists all organise their attention around moments, that a continuous stream of changes is indistinguishable from no change at all from outside the building, and that a company which never has a launch never has a narrative. The decoupling camp's evidence is the demonstrable reduction in release risk. The moment camp's evidence is that even the most aggressive continuous-delivery companies eventually reinstate an annual event, which suggests the need is real rather than nostalgic. The synthesis usually offered — "decouple release from launch" — is genuinely useful but it does not resolve the dispute, because it leaves open the hardest question: if the feature has been live for four months, what is the announcement about, and is the answer honest?

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic produces a wave plan. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in five observable ways.

First, she starts from the failure, not the calendar. Her first artefact is not a schedule but a short list of things that could go wrong, each with an estimated rate and an estimated cost per occurrence, and the schedule is derived from that list. When challenged on a wave size she gives an arithmetic answer, not a precedent.

Second, she reads the commitment ladder before the channel plan, and she knows which of her decisions are already made. She is therefore unsurprised when a gate closes and the money is gone anyway, and she has already told her CEO that this would be the case.

Third, she is comfortable saying that a particular launch should be a big bang. The competent practitioner has learned that staging is correct and applies it uniformly; the expert has learned the four conditions under which it is correct and can articulate, in a specific case, that the network-density condition fails and that a coordinated launch is therefore the lower-risk option. This is the single clearest behavioural marker, because it requires holding a view against the prevailing orthodoxy of one's own profession.

Fourth, she treats the claim as a dial alongside the channel and the audience. When she cannot stage exposure, she stages the promise; when she cannot stage the promise, she stages the guarantee, shipping with a remediation commitment rather than a weaker feature. She has three instruments where most people have one.

Fifth, and least visibly, she builds the authority structure before she builds the plan. She establishes, in writing and in advance, who can stop each wave, and she makes sure that person is senior enough to survive stopping it. She understands that a launch plan is a governance document that happens to contain dates, and that every elegant wave diagram in a company where nobody can say no is a drawing of a big bang with intermissions.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Sathe kept the congress. His argument to the commercial director, delivered on 18 September, was not that the congress was risky but that the congress was being asked to do two incompatible jobs — to be the first exposure and to be the moment of maximum claim — and that separating them made the congress better rather than worse. He ran Waves 1 through 3 quietly as a "clinical adoption programme", a framing that was accurate and that also preserved novelty by ensuring nothing about Patch 2 was publicly announced before January. When Wave 1 returned 0.75 per cent detachment with a confidence interval that cleared the threshold, he escalated at k = 4 rather than the 8 the schedule could have tolerated, on the grounds that the interval's upper bound of 1.42 per cent was uncomfortably close to the 1.5 per cent Wave 2 gate. The fourth wave and the congress happened together, with four thousand eight hundred completed studies of field data as the keynote's substance, and with the price change and the published adhesion results held back specifically for that room. What he did not do, and what he was explicit about internally, was pretend that the plan had de-risked the ₹4.72 crore. The inventory was always going to be the inventory. The plan bought him the difference between a phone call and a notification.

Qureshi kept the date and changed the claim. Hastakshar Review was enabled for all four hundred and thirty tenants on 19 November, as Menon wanted and as the partner's printed agenda promised, in advisory mode: an assistive summary with an explicit, visible statement that it did not assert completeness, and with the annexure-parsing weakness disclosed in the product itself rather than in a release note. The assertive mode — the version that feeds obligation extraction into downstream workflow and that Menon actually wanted to sell — was gated on a fresh twelve-hundred-document panel showing a miss rate below half a per cent, and it did not ship until the following quarter. The ₹10.81 lakh evaluation spend, which had been the most contentious line in the September budget review, became a permanent quarterly line item. Qureshi's summary of her own reasoning, offered at an internal review in December, was that she had spent ten lakh to discover that her informal estimate of the miss rate was wrong by a factor of two, and that the alternative to spending it was not saving it but shipping a completeness claim she could not support to forty banks.

Discussion questions

  1. Hridaya's staged plan reduced reputational and regulatory exposure substantially and reduced financial exposure not at all, because the inventory commitment preceded the waves by four months. What would have to change — in the supply agreement, in the product architecture, in the company's relationship with its contract manufacturer — for the financial bet to become stageable too? Would the cost of those changes have been worth paying?
  2. Hullor killed a good feature because a three per cent random wave measured an empty room. Its gate was written in advance, its instrumentation was clean, and its decision was disciplined — every rule in the orthodoxy was followed. What rule, stated generally, would have caught this, and can that rule be written in a form that does not simply give every team a licence to skip staging?
  3. Qureshi staged the claim rather than the audience, preserving a partner keynote while bounding liability. Under what circumstances is staging the claim dishonest rather than prudent — and who, inside a company, is positioned to tell the difference?

13. Going deeper

Channels: paid, owned, earned is the substrate this page assumes. Return to it with Figure 2 in mind: the three-way taxonomy is a good mnemonic and a poor risk model, and the upgrade is to characterise each channel by commitment lead time and recall half-life instead.

Crossing the chasm supplies the argument that the early market and the mainstream market are different populations, which is the correction to any launch plan that treats its first wave as a random sample. It unlocks the reasoning behind choosing Wave 1 by segment characteristics rather than by percentage.

Working with product marketing matters next because the claim — the third dial, alongside channel and audience — is drafted by product marketing, and a product manager who cannot negotiate the strength of a claim has surrendered the instrument Qureshi used to save her launch.

Launch tiers and launch readiness formalises the checklist that must clear before Wave 1 opens, and supplies the organisational machinery — tier definitions, readiness reviews, sign-off authority — that turns the governance point in section 11 into something a company can actually run.

Launching hardware: pre-orders, inventory, reviews is the deep treatment of the commitment ladder in Figure 3, and it unlocks the pre-order mechanism, which is the main instrument by which hardware companies convert an unstageable inventory bet into a partially stageable one.

Launch communications and PR is where novelty leakage is managed in practice: embargoes, exclusives, briefing sequences and the specific question of what can be said during a quiet staged wave without spending the coordinated moment.

Reading launch metrics honestly supplies the statistical discipline this page leans on throughout — confidence intervals on gate results, enthusiasm discounts on early cohorts, and the distinction between an absent signal and a bounded one.

What a GTM strategy is sits above launch planning and answers the prior question the launch plan assumes has been settled: which segment, which motion, which price. A launch plan cannot repair a wrong answer at that level.

Your first 100 users is the seed-stage special case where, as section 7 argued, the payoff matrix genuinely inverts and near-big-bang behaviour is often correct.

Inbound vs outbound determines the shape of the earned and owned waves in a B2B plan, and in particular whether Wave 1 can be executed by a marketing team at all or requires sales capacity that competes with the quarter's pipeline.

Product-led growth, sales-led growth and product-led sales (PQA / PQL) together determine what a "wave" even denotes in a given company: a cohort of self-serve users, a named account list, or a scored subset of existing users crossing an activation threshold. Hastakshar's tiering is a product-led-sales structure wearing a launch plan's clothes, and the reading on PQL scoring explains how the tier boundaries would be drawn if they were drawn quantitatively rather than by consequence of error.

Launch Planning and Launch Mistakes: Why the Best Launches Are Not Events

An Autumn Deadline

On the morning of 11 August 2026, Meera Iyer, VP of Growth Product at Aashray Money, sat in a glass conference room in Bengaluru's HSR Layout with a media plan she had not written and did not want to sign. Aashray Money ran a savings-and-micro-insurance app used by roughly 6.2 lakh gig workers — delivery riders, cab drivers, and platform-based technicians across twelve Indian cities — who linked the app to their weekly payouts from aggregators. The company's newest feature, Auto-Save, would automatically sweep a small, user-set percentage of every gig payout into an interest-bearing pot the moment the payout landed, using the UPI Autopay e-mandate rails that the National Payments Corporation of India had opened up to third-party apps two years earlier. It was, on paper, the best feature the product team had shipped: nine months of user research had shown that gig workers wanted to save but distrusted their own discipline to do it manually.

The plan on the table, drafted by the marketing agency and already blessed by the CFO, called for a single coordinated push on 2 October — Gandhi Jayanti, a national holiday with unusually high UPI transaction volumes — combining a regional television burst, a home-screen takeover on two major aggregator apps, and a nationwide push notification to every registered user at 9 a.m. sharp. The budget was ₹80 lakh, already committed to media bookings that could not be partially cancelled without forfeiting deposits. The CFO's argument was straightforward: Aashray had one shot at owning the "festival of savings" narrative, competitors were circling the same gig-worker segment, and a big, simultaneous moment would generate more press coverage than a series of small ones. Meera's discomfort was equally straightforward, though harder to put in a one-line memo: Auto-Save touched money, relied on a mandate-confirmation SMS that Aashray's engineering team had tested only against Airtel and Jio numbers, and had never been exposed to more than 400 real users at once. If something broke at the exact moment 6.2 lakh people saw a television ad telling them to turn it on, there would be no way to contain it, no channel left un-lit to quietly fix things through, and a regulator-sensitive product category in which "auto-debited money that didn't show up" was not a bug report but a front-page story. The question in front of her was not whether Auto-Save was ready to exist. It was whether a launch had to be a single, irreversible moment at all.

The Idea, Stated Plainly

A launch plan is a schedule that decides, in advance, which channels tell which audiences about a product and in what order — and, critically, what evidence must appear before the next channel is allowed to open. The three channel families a launch plan sequences are the same three that govern every marketing decision: owned channels, which the company controls completely and can switch off in minutes (its own app, push notifications, email list, website); earned channels, which the company influences but does not control (press coverage, word of mouth, community advocates, organic social sharing); and paid channels, which the company buys and can scale up or down but has usually pre-committed to, sometimes irreversibly (television slots, sponsored search, influencer contracts, billboard bookings). A launch plan's entire job is to answer one question in a disciplined order: given what we now know, which of these three should carry the message next, to how many people, and what result do we need to see before we let it grow?

The idea has no single inventor, but its modern shape owes most to two lineages that converged in the 2000s. The first is the product-led growth movement, visible in Gmail's 2004 invite-only rollout and later in Dropbox's referral-gated expansion, where engineering and support capacity, not marketing ambition, set the pace of exposure. The second is a much older idea from diffusion research, associated with the sociologist Everett Rogers: any population adopts something new in an S-curve, with a small segment of innovators and early adopters moving long before the mass market will touch it, so exposing the mass market before the early segment has validated the product wastes the one channel — a coordinated public moment — that a mass market actually needs. A launch plan simply operationalises that insight into a document with dates, channels, audiences and thresholds. The sentence Meera could say in the CFO's next meeting without sounding glib was this: a launch is not an event, it is a schedule of small, reversible bets across owned, earned and paid channels, each one sized so that a mistake discovered at that stage costs a week and a lakh, not a quarter and a crore.

Figure 1. A wave plan replaces one moment with a sequence of controllable, reversible ones, each gated on a metric agreed before the wave began.

The Mechanics of a Staged Launch

Building a wave plan is less about creativity than about ordering decisions that teams usually make in the wrong sequence under deadline pressure. The first step is to rank the three channel families not by cost or reach but by reversibility: how quickly, and how completely, can the company stop the message if something goes wrong? Owned channels rank highest — a push notification can be recalled or followed by a correction within the hour, and an in-app banner can be pulled the moment a support queue spikes. Earned channels rank in the middle: a community captain's WhatsApp group can be corrected quickly, but a newspaper article, once printed, cannot be un-published. Paid channels, especially broadcast and out-of-home media, rank lowest: a television slot is booked weeks ahead, non-refundable, and once it airs it has told everyone at once, with no way to whisper a correction to only the people who saw it. A wave plan simply launches in that order — owned first, earned second, paid third, with any large paid-plus-PR moment (a genuine big bang, if one is ever used) reserved for last and only after everything upstream has been validated.

The second step, and the one teams most often skip under time pressure, is writing the gate criteria before the wave opens, not after. A gate is a specific, numeric threshold that must be observed — a retention rate, a defect rate, a support-ticket ratio, a mandate-failure rate — that decides whether the next wave is allowed to proceed, is delayed for a fix, or is cancelled outright. If this number is decided only once the wave's real results are in, the team will unconsciously round the actual result up to whatever looks like success, because the pressure to keep the calendar moving is stronger after money has already been spent booking the next wave's media. Aashray's product, engineering, sales-operations and legal-compliance leads needed to sit in the same room before Wave 1 opened and sign off on the exact number — not "retention looks healthy" but "day-7 retention above 55 percent, mandate-confirmation failure rate below 1.5 percent" — that would open Wave 2.

The third step is instrumenting each wave so that its results can actually be attributed to it, which means every wave needs its own tracking link, promo code, or time window uncontaminated by another wave running in parallel. The fourth step, easy to state and hard to execute inside a company's budgeting culture, is holding back a genuine reserve rather than pre-committing the entire launch budget on day one. Aashray's CFO had booked all ₹80 lakh of media in advance partly because unspent quarterly budget is often clawed back the following year, an incentive that has nothing to do with the product and everything to do with how the finance calendar is structured — but it is precisely this incentive that pushes companies toward big-bang launches regardless of readiness. The final, and most frequently implicit, step is staffing a live cross-functional room for at least the first two waves: not a status update sent by email, but product, engineering, customer support, sales or channel-partner operations, and legal or compliance physically or virtually present together while the wave is live, because a mandate-failure incident in a regulated financial product needs a support-and-compliance response inside minutes, not inside the next sprint planning meeting.

The Arithmetic of Three Waves

Meera's team modelled the staged plan against the same ₹80 lakh budget the agency had already proposed spending in one shot. Table 1 shows the plan as built, wave by wave, with cost per activation defined as spend divided by the number of gig workers who actually turned Auto-Save on.

First, the blended cost per activation across the three spent waves is ₹43,00,000 divided by 17,400 activations, which comes to roughly ₹247 — a number nobody can see until the waves have actually run, because it depends on real click-through and real activation rates, not the agency's optimistic estimates. Second, notice that cost per activation rises by more than sixty times from Wave 1 to Wave 3: owned channels are nearly free because the audience already trusts the app and the infrastructure is sunk, while paid channels are buying attention from strangers who have to be persuaded from nothing, which is exactly why a sensible plan spends its cheapest, most controllable channel first and only escalates spend once the product has proven itself on a small, forgiving audience. During Wave 1, Aashray's support team noticed something the activation-rate number alone would never have shown: of the 10,800 people who turned Auto-Save on, only 35 percent were still saving by day seven, far below the 65 percent the product team had assumed from earlier pilot data. The root cause, traced within four days, was that the mandate-confirmation SMS silently failed for numbers on one telecom carrier, Vodafone Idea, whose delivery-receipt format Aashray's SMS gateway had never been tested against — so a meaningful share of users believed they had switched Auto-Save on when, technically, the recurring mandate had never been confirmed.
