Had Aashray run the big-bang plan as originally booked — owned and paid channels firing together on 2 October — the same Vodafone Idea mandate bug would have suppressed retained activations across the paid cohort as well, but the ₹35 lakh performance-marketing spend and the ₹80 lakh in total commitments would already be gone, the television slot already aired, and the true cost per retained activation would have jumped to roughly ₹890 instead of the ₹53 the staged plan actually paid to discover and fix the problem. Because the bug surfaced inside a wave of 10,800 people rather than a launch reaching all 6.2 lakh at once, Aashray fixed the SMS gateway configuration in six days, re-ran a corrected Wave 1 sample, confirmed 61 percent day-7 retention, and only then opened Wave 2. The mistake was the same size either way; what the wave structure changed was how much money and reputation were exposed to it before anyone noticed.

Eight Things a Careful Reader Should Notice

Staged is not the same as slow

The purpose of gates is to increase the rate at which the team learns true things about the launch, not to add caution for its own sake. A team that turns every gate into a two-week committee review has confused discipline with delay; the right gate duration is however long it takes the real signal — day-7 retention, mandate-failure rate — to become observable, and no longer.

Big-bang is not always the wrong answer

Some products genuinely need a coordinated moment: a two-sided marketplace introducing a new matching feature that only works once both sides adopt it simultaneously, or a change forced by a regulatory deadline that applies to every user on the same date, can make a single, simultaneous exposure the only workable design. The lesson is not "never launch everywhere at once," it is "do not default to it out of calendar convenience when the product has not earned that confidence."

The three channel families blur in practice

A referral programme looks earned because a friend is doing the recommending, but the company is paying for it through owned in-app credits; an influencer's post looks earned because it appears in a normal social feed, but it is contractually paid. The useful test is not what a channel looks like but who controls the message and how quickly that control can be withdrawn.

A launch plan is not a marketing plan

The marketing plan supplies the creative, the positioning and the messaging; the launch plan supplies the sequencing and the gating logic that decides when that creative is allowed to reach whom. A company can have brilliant creative and still fail badly by exposing it to the wrong audience size before the product has been tested against real behaviour.

What a launch plan cannot tell you

Sequencing channels well cannot compensate for a product that is not ready, nor can it tell you whether the market wants the feature at all — those are the jobs of launch-readiness review and of the discovery work that should have happened months earlier. A launch plan only manages the exposure of a decision that has already, separately, been judged sound.

Channel and audience segment are two different dials

The same owned channel, a push notification, can be aimed at power users in Wave 1 and at dormant users in a later wave; treating "wave" as synonymous with "channel" alone loses half the design space. A well-built plan crosses channel against segment deliberately, rather than assuming one channel means one audience.

Every added wave has a coordination cost

Each gate requires a sign-off meeting, a dashboard, and a delay while data accumulates; a mature team eventually learns which waves can be safely collapsed because the incremental information from separating them is not worth the calendar time, particularly for a feature type the company has already launched successfully several times before.

Waves are worthless without honest attribution

If two channels go live in overlapping windows with no distinct tracking, no one can honestly say which one produced the result, and teams under pressure to justify the next wave will retrofit a convenient story onto ambiguous numbers. Clean attribution has to be designed into the plan before Wave 1, not reconstructed afterward.

Consumer, B2B, Marketplace, and the Effect of Company Size

In a consumer product like Aashray Money, waves are naturally organised around geography and user segment, because the channels — push, referral, performance marketing — scale by audience size, and the binding constraint is usually operational: how many support tickets, mandate exceptions, or fraud reviews the back office can absorb per day. In a B2B product, the entire structure changes shape: a "wave" is a named tier of accounts rather than a percentage of an anonymous base, the earned channel is a customer advisory board or a handful of reference customers willing to be quoted, the owned channel is an in-product changelog plus direct outreach from the customer-success team, and paid channels barely matter compared with account-based marketing and, above all, whether the sales team itself has been trained to sell the feature. The gate in a B2B wave is rarely a click-through rate; it is closer to "can our top twenty sales reps explain this correctly on a call without a specialist on the line."

A marketplace complicates the picture further because it is two-sided: opening the same channel to both supply and demand at once frequently produces a marketplace with nothing on it, since demand encountering an empty supply side converts once and never returns. Marketplaces therefore often skip channel sequencing at the start entirely and instead sequence sides and geography — seeding one city's supply manually, sometimes literally by founders recruiting each vendor, before any channel, owned or paid, is opened to demand in that city at all. Only once supply density crosses a usable threshold does the conventional owned-earned-paid sequence begin, and it begins city by city rather than nationally.

Company size changes the arithmetic more than it changes the logic. An early-stage company has a thin owned channel simply because its user base is small, so its first wave is often forced into earned territory — founder-led outreach, niche communities, a handful of vocal early adopters — before it has any paid budget worth deploying at all, and its "war room" may be four people around a laptop rather than a scheduled cross-functional meeting, though the discipline of writing the gate down beforehand still has to hold. A large company has the opposite problem: its owned channel is so large in absolute terms that a "safe," single-digit-percentage first wave can still reach fifty thousand people, so wave sizing has to be expressed as a percentage of the base rather than an absolute headcount, and internal politics — multiple product lines competing for the same quarterly launch calendar slot, and the same finance-driven pressure to spend booked budget that Aashray's CFO faced — tends to push large companies toward big-bang defaults even when nothing about the product requires it.

Where Launch Plans Go Wrong

The first common mistake shows up as a launch dashboard that looks like a triumph on day one and a crisis two weeks later: sign-ups spike, then usage collapses and support tickets climb. The underlying misunderstanding is treating a one-time action — a registration, an opt-in — as the success metric instead of a retained, completed behaviour. The cheapest diagnostic is refusing to open any subsequent wave until the team has pulled day-7 or day-14 retention for the previous wave's cohort, not merely its day-1 conversion count.

The second shows up when marketing has locked a media slot and a press embargo months in advance, and when engineering flags a defect two days before the date, the launch proceeds anyway because the date feels immovable. The underlying misunderstanding is calendar-first thinking: treating the date as the fixed point and the product's readiness as the variable, when it should be the reverse. The cheapest diagnostic is a single question asked before any media is booked: "what result would make us not launch on this date?" If no honest answer exists, the date has already become a hostage rather than a gate.

The third shows up as a launch retrospective in which nobody can say which channel actually drove the activations that mattered. The underlying misunderstanding is running two or more channels in the same time window without distinct tracking, so the signals confound each other beyond separation. The cheapest diagnostic is checking, before any wave opens, whether it has an isolated attribution window of at least forty-eight hours before the next channel is scheduled to start.

The fourth shows up when a team declares victory at a round, appealing number — "ten thousand sign-ups!" — that was never written down as a gate criterion beforehand. The underlying misunderstanding is deciding success after the fact, under the pressure of a moving calendar, which is a textbook case of confirmation bias dressed up as a milestone. The cheapest diagnostic is requiring every wave's gate number to be written and signed by product, engineering and, for a regulated feature, legal, before that wave goes live — not afterward, when the incentive to round up has already taken hold.

Figure 2. The Vodafone Idea mandate defect existed either way; the wave structure decided whether it was found inside 10,800 people or inside the full base.

What the Second Week Looked Like When It Worked

A well-run version of this decision does not look dramatic from the outside, which is precisely why it is easy to under-value. In the week after Meera's Wave 1 launch, the room that had signed the gate criteria met every morning for eleven minutes: engineering reported the mandate-failure count from the previous twenty-four hours, support reported ticket volume and category, and product reported day-1 and, once available, day-7 retention against the agreed threshold. When the Vodafone Idea pattern appeared on day three, the meeting did not become a crisis negotiation about whether to still hit 2 October; it became a short technical conversation about a gateway configuration, because the gate criteria had already established, before anyone had an incentive to argue otherwise, that Wave 2 would not open until day-7 retention cleared 55 percent. Legal and compliance, present in the room from day one rather than looped in on launch morning, had already pre-approved the customer-communication template to use if a mandate failure was detected, so no one had to draft an apology message under pressure while regulators or the press were watching. By 15 September, a corrected Wave 1 sample confirmed 61 percent retention, Wave 2 opened in Pune, Jaipur and Indore exactly as scheduled with real confidence behind it, and the ₹37 lakh reserved for Wave 4 remained untouched, available for the CFO's original television idea if and when the numbers justified it.

Meera's Decision

Meera did not cancel the CFO's television plan; she reclassified it. She proposed, and the CFO agreed, to keep the ₹80 lakh commitment but restructure it as a reserve unlocked in stages rather than a single spend confirmed on a single date, converting a scheduling argument into a sequencing one that both sides could accept. Auto-Save launched to the existing base on 25 August, to three cities' worth of earned attention in early September, to national paid channels in mid-September once the corrected mandate-confirmation flow had proven itself at scale, and the television moment the CFO wanted happened after Diwali, in November, once genuine national numbers — a 3.9 lakh cumulative activation base with 58 percent 60-day retention — gave the campaign something true to say rather than something merely hoped for. The reasoning she carried into that meeting, and the one worth carrying into any launch meeting, was that a launch plan's job is not to make a company look decisive on a single morning; it is to convert an irreversible bet into a sequence of small, reversible ones, so that whatever a team does not yet know about its own product costs a wave, not the whole company's credibility.

The natural next things to study from here are Launch Tiers and Launch Readiness, which supply the checklist a product must clear before Wave 0 is even allowed to start, and Reading Launch Metrics Honestly, which supplies the discipline for telling a genuinely good gate result apart from a number that has been quietly redefined to look like one. Several MBA programmes, including INSEAD, IESE and SMU, teach this material through a launch role-play in which students playing product, sales, engineering and legal are placed in one room and forced to negotiate a gate criterion before they are told what the "real" data will show — a useful discipline, because writing the number down before you know the answer is the entire exercise.

Question 1. If your organisation's finance calendar penalises unspent budget, what would it take to redesign a launch's funding so that holding a reserve is rewarded rather than treated as a missed commitment?

Question 2. Think of the last launch you watched closely. Was there a written gate number that existed before the first wave opened — and if not, on what basis did anyone actually decide it was safe to go further?

Aaghaz Orchard Networks: The Season That Launches Itself

An ambiguous case on launch planning · Jammu, July 2027

1. Sunday night, 11 July 2027

The power went off in the Gandhi Nagar office at twenty past ten, and for the four seconds before the inverter caught, Ruchika Zutshi sat in the dark with her father's old grading card in her hand: a printed rectangle from the nineteen-nineties, colour patches for Kashmiri Delicious, a size gauge punched in three circles, a column for blemish tolerance. He had used it in a controlled-atmosphere store in Shopian until the season a chamber lost its compressor and four hundred boxes came out brown.

At ten the next morning Zutshi would present the 2027 launch plan for Aaghaz Peti to her board. It ran to fourteen slides and ₹82.00 lakh, and every number in it had been agreed by somebody who did not agree with anybody else. The Srinagar horticulture expo opened on 6 August. The first early varieties would move on 20 August. Her Dubai buyer needed digital grade certificates from 15 September. The chambers would seal on 20 November, and after that nothing anyone did would matter until August 2028.

What unsettled her was not the disagreement. It was a line in an email from Toronto that afternoon: three hundred and sixty-four people were already using the product she was preparing to launch, and nobody at Aaghaz had spoken to any of them.

2. How the company got here

Zutshi founded Aaghaz Orchard Networks in Jammu in March 2020, after seven years as a supply analyst for a Delhi grocery chain. Its first product, Aaghaz Store Book, was a chamber logbook for controlled-atmosphere stores: gas readings, box counts by grower and variety, dates in and out, and the paperwork a store needs when fruit leaves under a trader's name. It was unglamorous and it sold. By June 2027 it employed seventy-four people — forty-one in Jammu, eleven in Srinagar, nine in Udhampur, six in Kathua, five engineers in Bengaluru, a data scientist in Toronto and a finance head in Gurugram — on the revenue shown in Exhibit 1.

Two early decisions shaped everything after. The first was technical: in 2022, facing patchy orchard coverage and growers on ₹6,000 handsets, the team built grading on the WhatsApp Business API rather than an app — photograph a box, receive a suggested grade and a lot reference. Adoption was immediate and cheap. The cost, invisible for three years, was that Aaghaz could see messages but not sessions, cohorts, funnels or holdouts. Any question about who used what had to be answered by matching phone numbers by hand.

The second was contractual. In 2024 Aaghaz onboarded forty-two stores under a state horticulture mission grant paying two-thirds of the licence cost. Clause 9 required that any grading or marketing module built on the platform be available to all grant-assisted stores on the same terms and from the same date. Nineteen sit in the Jammu division, twenty-three in the valley. In 2024 the clause read like a marketing promise; in July 2027 it reads like a prohibition on staging.

3. The industry

India's apple economy runs on a chain that has barely changed in shape: grower, commission agent, mandi, cold store, wholesaler, retailer. Most of the crop comes from Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh, moves out through Sopore, Parimpora, Narwal and the Himachal mandis, and arrives at Azadpur in Delhi, still the price-setting market. The Agricultural Produce Market Committee system governs the mandi floor; eNAM has digitised parts of it; NAFED intervenes in bad years; Agmark defines grades the trade knows but few lots are certified against. FSSAI and APEDA sit on the export side.

What has changed is the buyer. Reliance Retail, DMart, BigBasket and the quick-commerce platforms want fruit that is uniform, dated and traceable, and will pay a premium for it; Tata and the large packers have built their own sorting lines; Iranian and Turkish imports, when duty and freight allow, cap the price of ungraded fruit. Consistency has become a commodity worth money — which is what Aaghaz Peti promises.

Standing between them is the commission agent: lender, broker and logistics provider at once, who advances money before harvest, takes the lot to the mandi and remits the proceeds minus six per cent. His margin depends partly on the grower not seeing what a lot fetched. Figure A sketches the three sides. 4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The marketplace idea arrived in 2025: if Aaghaz held the chamber ledger for 184 stores and a grading conversation with thousands of growers, it could list graded lots and take a fee. 8. The options as Zutshi sees them

Option A — the full season. Take the expo stage on 6 August, open all nine mandis and all 184 stores together, spend the ₹82.00 lakh of Exhibit 3. On the board case that transacts 15,624 lots and recovers 64.8 per cent of the spend; on the unattended case, 5,859 lots and 24.3 per cent. Either way the milestone is missed — at best 39.1 per cent of it — and the plan needs 490 engineer-days Exhibit 4 cannot supply.

Option B — valley first. Sopore, Parimpora and Shopian only, ₹41 lakh, Jammu division in 2028. The valley carried 7,800 of the 11,000 lots graded in 2026, or 70.9 per cent, so this is not obviously a small launch. At a reach of 38,000 growers and the unattended rates it transacts 3,591 lots for ₹12.21 lakh, 9.0 per cent of the milestone. Clause 9 makes the gating partly unenforceable: the nineteen grant stores in Jammu must be served anyway.

Option C — the buyer side first. No grower campaign in 2027; serve Bustan and two domestic chains through the 26 existing kiosks. ₹24 lakh of spend, 1,000 certified lots for Dubai at ₹14.40 lakh and 600 domestic lots at ₹900 each for ₹5.40 lakh: ₹19.80 lakh in all, 82.5 per cent of the spend recovered, the best unit economics of the three, and 4.0 per cent of the milestone. It means withdrawing Kachroo's briefings and giving up the stage.

Each option assumes the launch is an event Aaghaz schedules. Exhibit 6 says something started without it; Clause 9 says availability is not hers to phase; Figure B says the market sets the date. And all three put ₹18.00 lakh across 140 commission agents — ₹12,857 each — against an agent who moves 900 lots at ₹1.20 lakh, turning ₹10.80 crore, on which six per cent is ₹64.80 lakh. The incentive is 0.2 per cent of what the present arrangement pays him. Nobody has asked what a launch designed for the agent would look like, or whether Aaghaz Peti is one launch at all rather than three — a grading tool, a listing service and an export certificate — fused by marketing into a single brand and a single date.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10:00 IST on Monday 12 July. Expo bookings close 18 July; Kachroo's embargo expires 1 August; Darwish's certificates are due 15 September; chambers seal 20 November. Cash is ₹5.80 crore against ₹47 lakh a month, and the ₹12 crore tranche turns on 40,000 transacted lots that no version of Exhibit 5 reaches. Clause 9 binds forty-two stores to simultaneous availability. The DPDP gap removes 2,900 numbers from the cheapest channel Aaghaz owns. Charak will have eight engineers from 1 August whatever the plan says. And the 2022 WhatsApp architecture means that whatever Aaghaz does this season, it will not afterwards be able to prove which part of it worked.
